subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$:

$$x(x - 3) = 0$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $x = 0$
Mark 2: $x = 3$

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$ (correct to TWO decimal places):

$$2x^2 + 1 = 4x$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Standard form — $2x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0$
Mark 2: Correct substitution into the correct formula — $x = \dfrac{-(-4) \pm \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4(2)(1)}}{2(2)}$
Mark 3: $x = 1{,}71$
Mark 4: $x = 0{,}29$

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$:

$$x^2 - 2x - 3 > 0$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Factors — $(x - 3)(x + 1) > 0$
Mark 2: Critical values — $x = 3$ or $x = -1$
Marks 3–4 (double mark): $x < -1$ or $x > 3$ (i.e. $x \in (-\infty\,;\,-1) \cup (3\,;\,\infty)$)

Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Use of exponential law — $2^{2x} - 2^2 \cdot 2^x - 32 = 0$
Mark 2: Factors — $(2^x - 8)(2^x + 4) = 0$
Mark 3: $2^x = 8$
Mark 4: $2^x \neq -4$ (no solution)
Mark 5: Answer — $2^x = 2^3 \Rightarrow x = 3$

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$:

$$\sqrt{-2x + 4} - x = 2$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Isolating the root — $\sqrt{-2x + 4} = 2 + x$
Mark 2: Squaring both sides — $-2x + 4 = 4 + 4x + x^2$
Mark 3: Standard form — $x^2 + 6x = 0 \Rightarrow x(x + 6) = 0$
Mark 4: Answers with selection — $x = 0$ ($x \neq -6$)

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$ and $y$ simultaneously:

$$2x + y = 3$$
$$y^2 + xy = 2$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: From equation 1 — $y = 3 - 2x$
Mark 2: Substitution — $(3 - 2x)^2 + (3 - 2x)x = 2$
Mark 3: Standard form — $2x^2 - 9x + 7 = 0 \Rightarrow (2x - 7)(x - 1) = 0$
Mark 4: Both $x$-values — $x = \tfrac{7}{2}$ or $x = 1$
Mark 5: Both $y$-values — $y = -4$ or $y = 1$

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the product $\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{4}\right) \ldots$

Each factor in the product is of the form $\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n}\right)$ for $n \geq 2$.

Determine ALL the values of $n$ for which the product will be an integer value.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Telescoping product — $\dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{5}{4} \times \ldots \times \dfrac{n+1}{n} = \dfrac{n+1}{2}$
Mark 2: Statement — the product $\dfrac{n+1}{2}$ is an integer when $n + 1$ is divisible by $2$, i.e. $n \in \{3\,;\,5\,;\,7\,;\,\ldots\}$
Mark 3: $n$ must be an odd number, greater than $2$

subQuestions.questionText:
The first term of an arithmetic series is $7$. The common difference of this series is $5$ and the series contains $20$ terms.

Calculate the sum of this series.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}[2(7) + (20 - 1)(5)]$
Mark 2: Answer — $S_{20} = 1\,090$

subQuestions.questionText: The original arithmetic series is extended to $75$ terms. The sum of these $75$ terms is $14\,400$. Using sigma notation, write down an equation for the sum of the terms added to the original series.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: General term — $T_n = 7 + (n - 1)(5) = 5n + 2$
Mark 2: $S_{75} - S_{20} = 14\,400 - 1\,090$
Mark 3: Correct limits on the sigma notation — $\displaystyle\sum_{n=21}^{75}(5n + 2)$
Mark 4: $= 13\,310$, so $\displaystyle\sum_{n=21}^{75}(5n + 2) = 13\,310$
(Alternatively $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{55}(5n + 102) = 13\,310$, using $T_n = 102 + 5n$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
The sequence of the first differences of a quadratic pattern is: $1\,;\,3\,;\,5\,;\,\ldots$

If $T_{99}$ of this quadratic pattern is $9\,632$, calculate the value of $T_{98}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: The first differences form the sequence $T_n = 2n - 1$; the $98$th first difference $= 2(98) - 1 = 195$
Mark 2: Method — $T_{98} = T_{99} - (98\text{th first difference}) = 9\,632 - 195$
Mark 3: Answer — $T_{98} = 9\,437$

subQuestions.questionText: If it is further given that the third term of the quadratic pattern is $32$, determine the general term, $T_n$, of the quadratic pattern.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks — for $T_n = an^2 + bn + c$):
Mark 1: Second difference $= 2 \Rightarrow 2a = 2$
Mark 2: $a = 1$
Mark 3: $b = -2$ (from $3a + b = 1$)
Mark 4: Method to calculate $c$ — $9a + 3b + c = 32$ (or $T_3 = 1(3)^2 - 2(3) + c = 32$)
Mark 5: $c = 29$, so $T_n = n^2 - 2n + 29$

subQuestions.questionText:
A circle with radius $6$ cm is drawn. A second, smaller circle is drawn through the centre of the first circle and also touches the first circle internally, as shown in the diagram. A third, smaller circle is drawn through the centre of the second circle and touches the second circle internally. The process of drawing circles continues and forms a geometric pattern.

Write down the radius of the $3^{\text{rd}}$ circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — each circle's radius is half the previous one):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $2^{\text{nd}}$ circle $= \dfrac{6}{2} = 3$ cm, so $3^{\text{rd}}$ circle $= \dfrac{3}{2} = 1{,}5$ cm (or $6\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1{,}5$)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the sum of the areas of the first $10$ circles.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks — the areas form a geometric series $36\pi\,;\,9\pi\,;\,\tfrac{9}{4}\pi\,;\,\ldots$):
Mark 1: $a = 36\pi$
Mark 2: $r = \dfrac{1}{4}$
Mark 3: Substitution — $S_{10} = \dfrac{36\pi\left[\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^{10} - 1\right]}{\tfrac{1}{4} - 1}$
Mark 4: Answer — $S_{10} = 150{,}80$

subQuestions.questionText: Which circle has a diameter of $\dfrac{3}{128}$ cm?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks — the radii form $6\,;\,3\,;\,\tfrac{3}{2}\,;\,\ldots$):
Mark 1: Radius $= \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{128}\right) = \dfrac{3}{256}$
Mark 2: Equating to the general term — $\dfrac{3}{256} = 6\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$
Mark 3: Simplification — $\dfrac{1}{512} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1} \Rightarrow \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^9 = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$, so $n - 1 = 9$
Mark 4: Answer — $n = 10$ (the $10^{\text{th}}$ circle)
(Alternatively work with the diameters $12\,;\,6\,;\,3\,;\,\ldots$ and set $\dfrac{3}{128} = 12\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$, giving $n = 10$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Given: $f(x) = a^x - 1$ for $a > 0$. $B\left(2\,;\,\dfrac{-5}{9}\right)$ is a point on $f$.

Calculate the value of $a$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $-\dfrac{5}{9} = a^2 - 1 \Rightarrow a^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}$
Mark 2: Answer — $a = \dfrac{2}{3}$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the range of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $y > -1$ (i.e. $y \in (-1\,;\,\infty)$)

subQuestions.questionText: Sketch the graph of $f$. Clearly show the intercepts with the axes and asymptotes, if any.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Intercept $(0\,;\,0)$
Mark 2: Asymptote $y = -1$
Mark 3: Decreasing shape (since $0 < a < 1$)

subQuestions.questionText:
It is further given that C is a point on $f$ at $y = \dfrac{19}{8}$.

Determine the coordinates of $\text{C}'$, the image of C, when C is reflected about the line $y = x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $\dfrac{19}{8} = \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^x - 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{27}{8} = \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^x$, i.e. $\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)^3 = \left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)^{-x}$
Mark 2: Answer — $x = -3$, so $\text{C}\left(-3\,;\,\tfrac{19}{8}\right)$
Mark 3: Reflection about $y = x$ — $\text{C}'\left(\tfrac{19}{8}\,;\,-3\right)$

subQuestions.questionText:
Sketched below is the graph of $f(x) = \dfrac{a}{x + p} + q$ having the domain $(-\infty\,;\,1) \cup (1\,;\,\infty)$. The graph of $f$ cuts the $y$-axis at $(0\,;\,1)$. A line of symmetry of $f$ is given by $g(x) = x - 3$.

Write down the value of $p$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $p = -1$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the horizontal asymptote of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — the line of symmetry $g(x) = x - 3$ passes through the intersection of the asymptotes; the vertical asymptote is $x = 1$):
Mark 1: Substitution — $y = (1) - 3$
Mark 2: Answer — $y = -2$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the value of $a$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitute $(0\,;\,1)$ — $1 = \dfrac{a}{0 - 1} - 2 \Rightarrow 3 = \dfrac{a}{-1}$
Mark 2: Answer — $a = -3$

subQuestions.questionText: For which values of $x$ is $f(x) \geq 0$?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $x$-intercept — $\dfrac{-3}{x - 1} - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow -3 = 2x - 2 \Rightarrow x = -\tfrac{1}{2}$
Marks 2–3 (double mark): $x \in \left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\,;\,1\right)$ (i.e. $-\tfrac{1}{2} \leq x < 1$)

subQuestions.questionText:
Graph $f$ undergoes a transformation to $h$ where:

- The domain and range of $h$ are the same as that of $f$
- $h'(x)$, the derivative of $h$, is negative on its domain

Describe a possible transformation that $f$ could have undergone to result in $h$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $f$ is reflected in the $y$-axis, then translated $2$ units to the right (OR reflected in the $x$-axis, then translated $4$ units down; OR reflected about the line $x = 1$; OR reflected about the line $y = -2$)

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, the graphs of $f(x) = -x^2 + 4x + 5$ and $g$, a straight line, are drawn. $C(3\,;\,8)$ is a point of intersection of $f$ and $g$. EH is drawn parallel to the $y$-axis, with E a point on $f$ and H a point on $g$.

Calculate the coordinates of B, the turning point of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Method for $x$ — $x = \dfrac{-4}{2(-1)}$ (or $f'(x) = -2x + 4 = 0$)
Mark 2: $x = 2$
Mark 3: $y = -(2)^2 + 4(2) + 5 = 9$, so $B(2\,;\,9)$

subQuestions.questionText: Show that the equation of the line through A and C is given by $g(x) = 2x + 2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks — A is the left $x$-intercept of $f$):
Mark 1: $x^2 - 4x - 5 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 5)(x + 1) = 0$, so $A(-1\,;\,0)$
Mark 2: Method for gradient — $m = \dfrac{8 - 0}{3 + 1} = 2$
Mark 3: Substitute point A or C into the straight-line equation — $y - 0 = 2(x + 1) \Rightarrow y = 2x + 2$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the maximum length of EH for $f > g$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Difference — $EH = (-x^2 + 4x + 5) - (2x + 2)$
Mark 2: $EH = -x^2 + 2x + 3$
Mark 3: $x$-value of maximum — $-2x + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1$
Mark 4: Maximum length — $EH = -(1)^2 + 2(1) + 3 = 4$

subQuestions.questionText:
Given: $k(x) = f(x + m) = -x^2 - 2mx - m^2 + 4x + 4m + 5$

Determine the value of $m$ such that $g$ is a tangent to $k$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: $k'(x) = -2x - 2m + 4$
Mark 2: $k'(x) = 2$ (gradient of $g$)
Mark 3: $x = 1 - m$
Mark 4: Substitution — $k(1 - m) = g(1 - m)$, i.e. $-(1-m)^2 - 2m(1-m) - m^2 + 4(1-m) + 4m + 5 = 2(1-m) + 2$
Mark 5: Answer — $-2m - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow m = -2$
(Alternatively set $k(x) = g(x)$ and use $\Delta = 0$: $0 = x^2 + (2m - 2)x + m^2 - 4m - 3$, $\Delta = 8m + 16 = 0 \Rightarrow m = -2$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Mary's grandparents deposited $R5\,000$ into a savings account on the day that she was born. The account pays interest at a rate of $6{,}8\%$ p.a., compounded quarterly. Calculate the accumulated amount in this account on Mary's $16^{\text{th}}$ birthday.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Correct $i$ and $n$ — $i = \dfrac{6{,}8}{400}$, $n = 64$
Mark 2: Substitution into the correct formula — $A = 5\,000\left(1 + \dfrac{6{,}8}{400}\right)^{64}$
Mark 3: Answer — $A = R14\,706{,}56$

subQuestions.questionText: After $4$ years, the value of a printer was half of its original value. Determine the rate at which the value of the printer depreciated over this period, if depreciation was calculated according to a straight-line method.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution into the correct formula — $\tfrac{1}{2}P = P(1 - 4i)$, so $\tfrac{1}{2} = 1 - 4i$
Mark 2: Answer — $i = \tfrac{1}{8}$, so $r = 12{,}5\%$

subQuestions.questionText:
Tshepo was granted a loan of $R100\,000$ on 1 March 2022 at an interest rate of $13{,}5\%$ p.a., compounded monthly. Tshepo agreed to repay the loan over $5$ years in monthly instalments of $R2\,300{,}98$, starting on 1 April 2022.

Calculate the total interest that he will pay over the $5$ years.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Amount already paid — $2\,300{,}98 \times 60 = R138\,058{,}80$
Mark 2: Interest — $138\,058{,}80 - 100\,000 = R38\,058{,}80$

subQuestions.questionText: Tshepo paid $R22\,300{,}98$ (his monthly instalment and an additional $R20\,000$) on 1 March 2024 into the loan account. He continues to pay the original monthly instalment thereafter. How many months earlier will Tshepo repay the loan?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (7 marks):
Mark 1: $n = 36$ for the balance after 2 years
Mark 2: Correct $i = \dfrac{13{,}5}{1200}$
Mark 3: Substitution into the correct balance formula — $P = \dfrac{2\,300{,}98\left[1 - \left(1 + \tfrac{13{,}5}{1200}\right)^{-36}\right]}{\tfrac{13{,}5}{1200}} = R67\,804{,}94$
Mark 4: Balance after the $R20\,000$ payment — $67\,804{,}94 - 20\,000 = R47\,804{,}94$
Mark 5: Substitution into the correct formula — $47\,804{,}94 = \dfrac{2\,300{,}98\left[1 - \left(1 + \tfrac{13{,}5}{1200}\right)^{-n}\right]}{\tfrac{13{,}5}{1200}}$
Mark 6: Correct use of logs — $0{,}766 = (1{,}01125)^{-n}$
Mark 7: $n = 23{,}83$ (months of remaining payments), so the loan is repaid $12$ months earlier

subQuestions.questionText:
Determine:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[3x - 5x^2\right]$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $3$
Mark 2: $-10x$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[3x - 5x^2\right] = 3 - 10x$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine $g'(x)$ if $g(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^2} - \sqrt[3]{x^7}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $2x^{-2}$ (rewriting first term)
Mark 2: $-x^{\frac{7}{3}}$ (rewriting second term)
Mark 3: $-4x^{-3}$ (derivative of first term)
Mark 4: $-\dfrac{7}{3}x^{\frac{4}{3}}$ (derivative of second term), so $g'(x) = -4x^{-3} - \dfrac{7}{3}x^{\frac{4}{3}}$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the tangent to $f(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + 2x + 3$ at $x = 2$.

Given: $f(x) = -6x^2$

Determine $f'(x)$ from first principles.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $f'(x) = \displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{-6(x + h)^2 + 6x^2}{h}$
Mark 2: $f(x + h) = -6x^2 - 12xh - 6h^2$
Mark 3: Simplification — $\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{-12xh - 6h^2}{h}$
Mark 4: Common factor — $\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{h(-12x - 6h)}{h} = \displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}(-12x - 6h)$
Mark 5: Answer — $f'(x) = -12x$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down how you will restrict the domain of $f$ such that $f^{-1}$, the inverse of $f$, is a function.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $x \geq 0$ (or $x \leq 0$)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of $f^{-1}$ for $f^{-1}(x) \leq 0$. Write your answer in the form $y = \ldots$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Swopping $x$ and $y$ — $x = -6y^2$
Mark 2: $y = \pm\sqrt{-\tfrac{1}{6}x}$
Mark 3: Answer with selection — $y = -\sqrt{-\tfrac{1}{6}x}$ (for $x \leq 0$)

subQuestions.questionText:
$A(1\,;\,9)$ and $B\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\,;\,8\right)$ are the turning points of graph $f$ below. $C(0\,;\,7)$ is the $y$-intercept of $f$.

For which values of $x$ is $f$ decreasing?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $1 < x < \dfrac{5}{2}$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the $x$-intercepts of $f'$, the derivative of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — the $x$-intercepts of $f'$ are the $x$-values of the turning points of $f$):
Mark 1: $x = 1$
Mark 2: $x = \dfrac{5}{2}$

subQuestions.questionText: For which values of $x$ will $f$ be concave up?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — the point of inflection is the midpoint of the turning points):
Mark 1: Method — $\dfrac{\tfrac{5}{2} + 1}{2} = \dfrac{7}{4}$
Mark 2: Answer — concave up for $x > \dfrac{7}{4}$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the value of $k$ for which $y = f(x) + k$ will have THREE positive $x$-intercepts.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — shifting $f$ vertically so all three roots become positive; the lower turning point $y = 8$ must move to $0 < y$ and the $y$-intercept $7$ must move below the $x$-axis):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $-9 < k < -8$

subQuestions.questionText:
A cyclist rode from town P and stopped at town T. The speed (in km/h) at which this cyclist rode is represented by the equation $s'(t) = -3t^2 + 18t$.

**NOTE:** Speed is the rate of change in distance with respect to time.

Calculate the maximum speed that the cyclist reached on this ride.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $s''(t) = -6t + 18 = 0$
Mark 2: Value of $t$ — $t = 3$
Mark 3: Answer — $s'(3) = -3(3)^2 + 18(3) = 27$ km/h

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the distance between town P and town T.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks — the cyclist stops when the speed is $0$):
Mark 1: Factors — $-3t^2 + 18t = 0 \Rightarrow -3t(t - 6) = 0$
Mark 2: Values — $t = 0$ or $t = 6$
Mark 3: $a$ and $b$ from $s'(t) = 3at^2 + 2bt$ — $a = -1$ and $b = 9$
Mark 4: Substitution — $s(t) = -t^3 + 9t^2$, so $s(6) = -(6)^3 + 9(6)^2$
Mark 5: Answer — $s(6) = 108$ (distance $= 108$ km)

subQuestions.questionText:
A certain number of learners are sitting for examinations in Mathematics, Tourism and Geography.

- All these learners sit for at least one of these examinations.
- The total number of learners who sit for Mathematics (M), is $22$.
- The total number of learners sitting for Tourism (T), is $16$.
- The total number of learners sitting for Geography (G), is $18$.
- $5$ learners sit for Mathematics and Tourism, but not Geography.
- $4$ learners sit for Mathematics and Geography, but not Tourism.
- $3$ learners sit for Tourism and Geography, but not Mathematics.
- $6$ learners sit for only Tourism.

Draw a Venn diagram to represent ALL the learners sitting for these examinations.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks — let the centre (all three) $= x$):
Mark 1: Centre value — $x = 2$ (from T total: $6 + 5 + 3 + x = 16$)
Mark 2: Values $3\,;\,4\,;\,5$ in the two-subject regions (M∩T only $= 5$, M∩G only $= 4$, T∩G only $= 3$)
Mark 3: Values $6\,;\,9\,;\,11$ in the single-subject regions (M only $= 11$, T only $= 6$, G only $= 9$); total $= 40$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the probability that a learner, chosen at random, will sit for examinations in at least TWO of the subjects.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Numerator — $(4 + 2 + 5 + 3) = 14$
Mark 2: Denominator $40$, so $P(\text{at least two subjects}) = \dfrac{14}{40} = \dfrac{7}{20} = 0{,}35$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine if the events: sitting for examinations in Mathematics and sitting for examinations in Tourism are independent. Support your answer with the necessary calculations.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $P(M) \times P(T) = \dfrac{22}{40} \times \dfrac{16}{40}$
Mark 2: $= \dfrac{11}{50} = 0{,}22$
Mark 3: $P(M \text{ and } T) = \dfrac{7}{40} = 0{,}175$
Mark 4: Since $P(M) \times P(T) \neq P(M \text{ and } T)$, events M and T are NOT independent

subQuestions.questionText:
A company generates a 4-character code using the 26 letters of the alphabet and the 10 digits, from 0 to 9.

The code is in the form:

| letter | digit | letter | digit |
|---|---|---|---|

Determine how many different codes can be formed if letters and digits may be repeated.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Correct letters — $26 \times 26$
Mark 2: Correct digits — $\times 10 \times 10$, so $26 \times 10 \times 26 \times 10 = 67\,600$

subQuestions.questionText:
Determine how many different codes can be formed if:

- The letters D, F, I, Q, U and V may NOT be used
- The code may NOT start with a W or a Z
- Letters or digits may NOT be repeated
- The code ends with an odd digit
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks — $20$ usable letters; first letter excludes W and Z; last digit is odd):
Mark 1: First position (letter, not W or Z) — $18$
Mark 2: Second position (digit) — $9$
Mark 3: Third position (letter, no repeat) — $19$
Mark 4: Fourth position (odd digit) — $5$; total $= 18 \times 9 \times 19 \times 5 = 15\,390$

subQuestions.questionText: The company wishes to increase the number of 4-character codes formed in QUESTION 12.2 by allowing the letters D, F, I, Q, U and V to be used. Calculate the percentage increase in the number of different codes that can now be formed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — now $26$ letters, first letter still excludes W and Z, so $24$):
Mark 1: New total — $24 \times 9 \times 25 \times 5 = 27\,000$
Mark 2: Percentage increase — $\dfrac{27\,000 - 15\,390}{15\,390} \times 100 = 75{,}44\%$
